claims.text: The additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has a primarily homogeneous FCC matrix.
The as-manufactured alloy may contain minor microsegregation or porosity.
Gas environment governs degradation of this alloy during elevated-temperature exposure.
Oxidizing conditions cause rapid selective oxidation of elements such as Al and Cr.
Selective oxidation produces a thick, poorly adherent oxide scale.
Poor oxide adhesion and thermal-expansion mismatch cause scale spallation and stress concentrations.
Oxide-scale spallation promotes surface crack initiation and propagation.
Surface-scale formation, scale adhesion, and associated grain-boundary oxidation influence internal microstructural integrity.
Reducing conditions prevent formation of a sufficiently robust passivating scale.
The absence of a robust passivating scale under reducing conditions permits internal diffusion and compositional changes.
Internal diffusion and compositional changes under reducing conditions produce phase modifications or brittle phases.
The phase changes produced under reducing conditions embrittle the alloy and reduce its ductility.
Oxidizing exposure will produce thicker, less adherent scales and more rapid cracking than the unexposed baseline.
Reducing exposure will produce relatively subtle surface features but detectable internal phase changes and reduced ductility.
Both oxidizing and reducing exposures will cause earlier catastrophic failure than in the as-manufactured baseline.
The proposed degradation behavior applies to prolonged exposure near 800°C in sufficiently oxidizing or reducing atmospheres.
Temperatures outside the stated range or atmospheres with weaker gas reactivity may not produce the same degradation mechanisms.
